native_result.query: How does the effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP compare between developing countries and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: Based on the 1975–2015 World Development Indicators regional-aggregate data, the association between increases in education expenditure — measured by the only education-spending series present, "Adjusted savings: education expenditure (% of GNI)" — and per capita income growth is weak and, for the lower-middle-income group (LMC), specification-dependent rather than robustly positive. In the LMC arm (treated as the "developing countries" arm per the study context — a stated assumption, not a fact), the leading year-over-year growth-form regression (Δln GNI per capita ~ Δ education expenditure, 1992–2015, n=24) gives a small positive coefficient of 0.028 (p<0.001, R²≈0.02): a 1-percentage-point increase in the education-spending share is associated with only about a 2.7% higher per capita GNI, and the association flips sign when enrollment, labor-force-participation and exports-growth controls are added (−1.05, p=0.05); the levels-form association is positive bivariate but insignificant with controls. In the Sub-Saharan Africa arm (file code SSF), per capita GNI exists only for 2011–2015 (n=5), so the "effect" is a descriptive slope/correlation, not a regression estimate: education spending fell ~0.12 percentage points per year while per capita GNI grew ~1.2% per year (within-window level correlation ≈ −0.97), i.e., no positive contemporaneous association in that short window. Accordingly, the data do not support a robust positive effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita income growth in either group; the LMC bivariate growth-form association is small, positive but fragile, and the SSA short-window trend is negative, making the cross-group comparison asymmetric (a regression coefficient versus a 5-point descriptive trend). This conclusion is limited by the regional-aggregate (not country-level) data, the associational (not causal) nature of the analysis, and the 2011–2015 income window for Sub-Saharan Africa.

Reshaped to year-indexed series per group. LMC arm (assumed 'developing countries'): group-specific OLS over 1991–2015 common support (all six variables present) — growth-form lead Δln(GNI/cap) ~ Δ(Adjusted savings: education expenditure, % of GNI), n=24, plus growth-form with lagged spending, growth- and levels-form with controls (primary/secondary enrollment, LFP, exports growth), and 1975–2015 full-period robustness. SSA arm (SSF): per-capita GNI available only 2011–2015 (n=5), so descriptive slopes/correlations only (no regression). Cross-group comparison of the LMC regression coefficient against the SSA short-window trend, with spending-level and income-growth context. Full output in analysis_output.txt.
